subject: space
title: Planet Cards
summary: Eight planets, eight cards — a flip-through deck that turns every planet into a readable fact sheet: what it's made of, how big it is, how far from the Sun, how long its day and year last, and how strong its gravity is. Pick any two cards to compare side by side and see how the planets sort into two families: small rocky worlds and huge gas or ice giants.

compareCandidate.label: Rocky planet vs. gas giant
compareCandidate.description: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are small, dense, rocky worlds with solid surfaces. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are enormous worlds of gas and ice with no solid surface to stand on — comparing one of each family makes the two types of planet impossible to confuse.

Compare two cards side by side

processes: Sorting planets into families by composition
Relating day length to spin and year length to distance
Using Earth as the reference for every comparison
plainLanguageExplanation: A planet card is like a baseball card, but for a world: one side is a picture, and the other is a list of stats. Every planet has a card in this deck, and every card uses the same rows — what the planet is made of, its radius compared to Earth, its distance from the Sun in AU, how long one day lasts, how long one year lasts, its surface gravity compared to Earth, and how many moons it has. Because every card uses the same rows, you can lay two cards side by side and compare any row directly: Earth's day is 24 hours, Mars's is 24.6 hours, Jupiter's is under 10 hours. The deck also sorts itself into two families automatically: the four inner planets are rocky worlds, and the four outer planets are gas giants (Jupiter and Saturn) and ice giants (Uranus and Neptune). When you flip through the deck, watch how day length, year length, and gravity each follow their own pattern — that's the beginning of reading planets like data, the way astronomers do.

whyItMatters: Astronomers cannot visit most planets, so they learn about worlds by comparing rows of data — exactly what this deck does. The skill of reading a table and spotting patterns (rocky planets are small, gas giants are huge, outer planets have long years) transfers directly to real science: it is how scientists decide which exoplanets might be Earth-like, and it is how mission planners decide which worlds to visit next. Learning to see planets as data instead of just pictures is the first step toward thinking like an astronomer.
didYouKnow: If you lined up every planet card by day length, Jupiter would win with a day under 10 hours — the biggest planet spins the fastest of all.
compareReason: The cards report sizes as numbers; the Planet Size Comparison component draws those same numbers as real spheres — together they connect the data row to the visual fact.
